You previously formulated the following research problem for the target paper.

Research problem: MVFA's few-shot image and pixel scores are produced by min-max normalising the zero-shot and the few-shot branch over the entire test set and adding them with weight 0.5, so the score of one image — and the ranking that defines the reported AUROC — depends on which other images are in the test set. How large is this dependence, and can it be removed by an inductive, per-image fusion that normalises each branch with statistics computed only from the K normal support images (leave-one-out scores of the supports against the memory bank and against the text anchors), together with a robust image-level aggregation (top-k mean instead of the max over the fused map)? Outcomes: (i) the spread of MVFA's fused AUROC across random sub-samples of the test set and under shifted prevalence (10% and 50% abnormal), (ii) image-level and pixel-level AUROC of the inductive fusion versus the transductive original, and (iii) sensitivity at 95% specificity, F1 and expected calibration error at a threshold fixed from the support scores alone, for every held-out BMAD modality and K in {2, 4, 8, 16}.
Rationale: The code verification changed this group of limitations: MVFA does normalise its branches (G8), but with test-set extremes, which makes the method non-deployable on a stream of single images and makes the reported numbers depend on the test set's composition; the image score is a max over the fused map for some datasets and a mean for others (G9, G17), and only AUROC is reported (G11). Related work concentrates on better representations and prompts (MLCA, ClipMPCAD, AnomalyCLIP, HieClip) and evaluates with the same threshold-free AUROC; AnomalyGPT removes thresholds only with a fine-tuned large vision-language model. The K normal support images are a label-free, per-modality reference that MVFA already loads but never uses for normalisation, which makes an inductive fusion possible without new data. The problem is confined to the scoring code (test_few.py), is inference-only on retrained baseline checkpoints, and measures exactly the deployment property — a per-image score with a transferable threshold — that the current evaluation hides.

- Relevance: rating 5/5. Review: Highly relevant: the verified code shows that MVFA's reported few-shot AUROCs depend on test-set extremes and that the method cannot score single images, which matters both for the validity of the published comparison and for deployment. Feedback: Note whether other CLIP-based baselines (e.g., APRIL-GAN) share the practice, which would broaden relevance.
- Originality: rating 4/5. Review: Quantifying how much a reported AUROC depends on transductive test-set normalisation is an unusual and useful perspective, and using the support normals as an inductive normalisation reference is a fresh, label-free idea, although score standardisation and top-k pooling themselves are classical. Feedback: Keep the emphasis on the evaluation-validity question and on the support-based reference, which are the novel parts.
- Feasibility: rating 5/5. Review: Inference-only changes to test_few.py on retrained baseline checkpoints; subsampling and prevalence-shift analyses are cheap. Feedback: With K = 2 the leave-one-out statistics come from very few patches per level; pool patch scores across levels if needed.
- Significance: rating 4/5. Review: Results bear on the trustworthiness of the published few-shot numbers and on whether MVFA can be deployed at all on a stream of images; the inductive fusion, if it matches the original AUROC, removes a hidden dependency at no cost. Feedback: Report how often conclusions from the paper's tables would change under inductive scoring.

Target paper title: Adapting Visual-Language Models for Generalizable Anomaly Detection in Medical Images
Target paper abstract: Recent advancements in large-scale visual-language pre-trained models have led to significant progress in zero-/few-shot anomaly detection within natural image domains. However, the substantial domain divergence between natural and medical images limits the effectiveness of these methodologies in medical anomaly detection. This paper introduces a novel lightweight multi-level adaptation and comparison framework to repurpose the CLIP model for medical anomaly detection. Our approach integrates multiple residual adapters into the pre-trained visual encoder, enabling a stepwise enhancement of visual features across different levels. This multi-level adaptation is guided by multi-level, pixel-wise visual-language feature alignment loss functions, which recalibrate the model's focus from object semantics in natural imagery to anomaly identification in medical images. The adapted features exhibit improved generalization across various medical data types, even in zero-shot scenarios where the model encounters unseen medical modalities and anatomical regions during training. Our experiments on medical anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models, with an average AUC improvement of 6.24% and 7.33% for anomaly classification, 2.03% and 2.37% for anomaly segmentation, under the zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively. Source code is available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD
Limitations to address:
- G8. Score fusion relies on test-set statistics and fixed weights; hyper-parameters are under-ablated: Numerous design choices (gamma = 0.1, lambda = 1.0, four feature levels, input resolution 240, learning rate 1e-3, 50 epochs, fixed prompt templates) are presented without sensitivity analysis. In the few-shot branch fusion, the paper describes adding scores on different scales; the released code instead min-max normalises each branch using the minimum and maximum over the ENTIRE TEST SET before fusing them with a fixed weight of 0.5. This normalisation is transductive: it cannot score a single incoming image, and the fused score of an image changes with the composition (e.g. prevalence, outliers) of the rest of the test set.
- G9. Image-level aggregation is inconsistent and outlier-sensitive: The image-level score is computed differently in training and testing and across datasets: training mean-pools the detection map; for datasets with masks, the reported image AUC uses the MAX over the fused segmentation map, so a single spurious high-scoring pixel decides the image label; for datasets without masks, mean-pooled detection scores are used. No robust aggregation, calibration or uncertainty estimate is used.
- G11. Metrics are too narrow for clinical readiness: Only image-level and pixel-level AUC are reported. The paper does not report Dice, IoU, or PRO scores; thresholded accuracy, F1, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, or NPV; false positives per patient; calibration or expected calibration error (ECE); or prevalence-adjusted and rare-category performance. AUC alone can obscure poor performance under severe class imbalance and does not by itself demonstrate clinical utility.
- G17. Paper and code disagree on image-level pooling: Eq. (3) of the paper defines the image-level loss with a max over the h x w anomaly map, while the released code mean-pools. Results in the paper therefore cannot be attributed to the method as described, and the effect of the pooling choice on detection is unknown.

Problem: Can MVFA's few-shot fusion be made inductive — scoring each image on its own, without the test-set min-max normalisation in the released code — without losing AUROC, and does this give a threshold that transfers to unseen modalities? The inductive fusion standardises each branch using leave-one-out statistics of the K normal support images (each support's zero-shot map, and its few-shot map against a memory bank built from the other K-1 supports, pooled over patches and levels), adds the standardised branches, and pools the fused map with the mean of its top 2% pixels; the threshold is the 95th percentile of the supports' leave-one-out image scores. Primary outcome: image- and pixel-level AUROC of inductive versus transductive fusion on every held-out modality and K in {2, 4, 8, 16}. Motivating measurement: the spread of the transductive AUROC across random test subsets and at 10% and 50% prevalence. Secondary outcomes: sensitivity at the support-derived threshold, realised specificity, F1 and expected calibration error.

Rationale: Reviewers asked to single out the primary question and to define the leave-one-out statistics exactly. The primary question is now whether per-image (deployable) scoring matches the published transductive scoring; the test-set dependence analysis motivates it, and thresholded metrics are secondary. The leave-one-out procedure is fully specified, including pooling across levels to keep K = 2 well-defined. The change is confined to test_few.py, needs no training beyond re-running the baseline under the shared protocol, and directly addresses the verified limitations G8, G9, G11 and G17.
